differences.what: the detailed point-by-point statement that the method is not the white-bear stance, specifying the white-bear stance's contrast (think/don't-think toward a named concept on a neutral carrier) and its effective depth (layers 20-24)
differences.message_quote: The white-bear stance (the existing method in `papers/`) has a **threshold** effect — flat to total push ≈13, then 0.29→0.83 — because it makes the model qualitatively *start writing* the concept.
differences.writeup_quote: It is not the white-bear stance (raman2026): that contrasts a *think / don't-think stance* toward a *named* concept, captured on a *neutral* carrier, at layers 20–24.

message_source_quote: The white-bear stance (the existing method in `papers/`) has a **threshold** effect — flat to total push ≈13, then 0.29→0.83 — because it makes the model qualitatively *start writing* the concept.
writeup_source_quote: It is not the white-bear stance (raman2026): that contrasts a *think / don't-think stance* toward a *named* concept, captured on a *neutral* carrier, at layers 20–24.
rationale: Both documents name the white-bear/raman2026 source and treat completion steering as a genuinely new method that nonetheless falls short of the source's performance because it lacks the source's threshold-trigger property. The write-up goes further, stating explicitly that the gain flows through 'the same channel the white-bear paper identifies' and gives a precise point-by-point contrast (think/don't-think over a named concept, neutral carrier, layers 20-24) against the source, whereas the message only references the threshold effect and omits the shared-channel/mechanistic-overlap claim and the precise characterization of the source's method, making the message's account of overlap and novelty less complete than the write-up's.
